where: Section 1, third bullet ("the two inputs do not look alike")
problem: This describes the four-resistor difference amplifier wrongly, and contradicts the first bullet of the same section and the answer to Q4. In the difference amplifier both sources are loaded by a resistor R₁ (one goes to the virtual node at the inverting input, the other to the non-inverting input which also has R₁ to ground), so neither input is "a high-resistance op-amp input". The description given belongs to the two-op-amp instrumentation amplifier (Section 3), not to a plain difference amplifier.
fix: Third, its two inputs load the source in a way that depends on the source resistances: each input shunts the source with about R₁, and if the two source resistances are unequal the two dividers are unequal, so common-mode noise turns into a false differential signal.

problem: The text says the bridge, thermocouple or skin electrode "asks for four things" but only three items are listed (high input resistance, gain set by one resistor, CMRR above 100 dB).
fix: Either write "three things", or list four separately: a high input resistance (above 10⁹ Ω), the same resistance on both inputs, gain set by one resistor, and CMRR above 100 dB.

problem: "the first stage's very high value" is inaccurate. The input stage has common-mode gain exactly 1 and differential gain 1 + 2R/R_G, so its own CMRR is only 1 + 2R/R_G (60 dB at a gain of 1000, 0 dB when R_G is open). What makes the first stage harmless is that its common-mode gain is 1, not a very high CMRR.
fix: CMRR: the input stage passes the common mode at gain 1, so it does not limit the CMRR. The overall CMRR is set by the matching of the second-stage resistors (or, in a monolithic part, by their on-chip trimming): 100 dB to 120 dB at gain 10. Build the same circuit from discrete op-amps and the second-stage resistors decide the CMRR, however good the op-amps are.

problem: "take the shield from the R_G node" is ambiguous and, read literally, wrong: R_G has two ends, one sitting at v₁ and the other at v₂, so a shield connected there would be driven by the signal itself and its capacitance would be charged by the signal. A driven shield must follow the common-mode voltage.
fix: Drive the cable shield from the common-mode voltage: the midpoint of R_G if R_G is made of two equal halves, or the average of the two buffer outputs. The shield then moves with the common mode, not with the signal, so cable capacitance is not charged by the signal.

problem: The question says only that the four second-stage resistors are equal; it never gives a value. The answer inserts 10 kΩ ("10 kΩ/10 kΩ = 1"), which is a number the student cannot know from the question.
fix: Second stage: all four resistors are equal, so R_f/R₁ = 1. Total A_d = 99.8 × 1 ≈ 100.

problem: The label "1 + 2R/R_G" is placed on the buffer→R_G edge, which suggests the signal (and the gain) passes through R_G into the next block, and R_G has no onward edge. Students may read the gain as coming out of R_G instead of out of the two buffers.
fix: Put the label "1 + 2R/R_G" on the two buffer→diff-amp paths (or as a note on the whole buffer pair) and leave the R_G edges unlabelled.

problem: "Strain-gauge weighings" is not idiomatic English and is vague for a second-language reader.
fix: Strain-gauge load cells in weighing scales, ECG and EEG front ends, thermocouples and shunt current sensing all use it.
